summary:
Mission X Spark is a free, mobile-first browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. Players run a Moon and Mars outpost for 10 days and manage three resources: power, oxygen and radiation safety. No download or account is needed.

It answers the challenge by turning real mission constraints into gameplay. Every decision has a cost. Boosting radiation shielding uses power that life support needs, and an extra experiment earns science points but strains oxygen. Solar storm events are based on real NASA space weather data (DONKI), so kids see how real solar activity affects survival. Events vary between playthroughs, and when a mission fails the game explains why, so kids learn from it.

It matters because most space content for kids shows the outcomes of missions, not the decisions behind them. Mission X Spark lets children experience the trade-offs that astronauts and mission planners handle, in plain language, with sources credited. They leave understanding that no choice in deep space is free.
details:
Mission X Spark is a mobile-first astronaut mission game for kids aged 7-12. Players act as junior astronauts running a Moon and Mars outpost over a 10-day mission. Each day they make decisions to balance three critical resources: power, oxygen, and radiation safety. We want to spark curiosity about space and science in young learners and show that space exploration depends on careful decisions as much as on rockets. By connecting gameplay to live NASA data, kids learn that space science is real, current, and something they could contribute to one day.

Tools and technologies

Deployment: Vercel (web hosting), with a custom domain at missionxspark.space https://mission-x-spark.vercel.app/

Front end: HTML, CSS, JavaScript [ e.g., React/Next.js, and any game or animation libraries]

Data: NASA space weather data ['DEMO_KEY', e.g., NASA DONKI, if that’s what you used]

Design: Mobile-first, responsive layout with a dark “space” theme [add design tools, e.g., Figma, Canva]

Hardware: Developed on [laptops/phones]; it runs on phones, tablets, and computers

It turns real, live NASA data into game events, so the game is never just a fixed script.

Balancing three competing resources creates real trade-offs: using more power may protect the crew, but it can drain oxygen.

Kids take on the role of mission commander rather than just answering quiz questions.

The Moon-to-Mars setting connects to NASA’s current exploration goals.

Age-appropriateness: Simple language, clear visuals, and a 10-day structure that is short enough to finish.

Accessibility: Mobile-first design, since many kids use phones or tablets, and no sign-up so there is no barrier to playing.

Scientific accuracy: Using real NASA data while simplifying concepts without making them wrong.
